source.title: Finite translation generalized quadrangles: old results, new results, open problems

accepted.question_text: Let O(n, n, q) be a pseudo-oval, meaning a set of q^n + 1 mutually constrained (n − 1)-dimensional subspaces in PG(3n − 1, q) as defined in the paper. Is every such pseudo-oval regular, in the sense of arising from the paper’s field-extension construction of a regular pseudo-oval?

evidence.quote: 1. Is any O(n, n, q) regular?
For n = m such a set O(n, n, q) is called a pseudo-oval or a generalized oval or an [n − 1]-oval of PG(3n − 1, q).
Here, we speak of a regular pseudo-oval, respectively a regular pseudo-ovoid.

accepted.question_text: If O is a translation generalized oval in PG(3n − 1, q) with q even—that is, a generalized oval for which there is a group of involutions fixing O and acting regularly on all elements except one distinguished element—is O necessarily regular?

evidence.quote: 2. Is any translation generalized oval regular?

Then O is a translation generalized oval, with axis the tangent space PG(i)(2n − 1, q) of O at PG(i)(n−1, q) ∈ O, if there is a group of involutions of PGL(3n, q) with axis PG(i)(2n − 1, q), fixing O and acting regularly on O − {PG(i)(n − 1, q)}.
Here, we speak of a regular pseudo-oval, respectively a regular pseudo-ovoid.

accepted.question_text: For a pseudo-oval O(n, n, q) in odd characteristic, is O always isomorphic to its translation dual O∗(n, n, q), where O∗ is the pseudo-oval formed by the tangent spaces of O in the dual projective space?

evidence.quote: 3. Is O(n, n, q), q odd, always isomorphic to its translation dual O∗(n, n, q)?
For n = m such a set O(n, n, q) is called a pseudo-oval or a generalized oval or an [n − 1]-oval of PG(3n − 1, q).
In the dual space of PG(3n − 1, q) the qn + 1 tangent spaces of O form a pseudo-oval O∗ = O∗(n, n, q). This pseudo-oval O∗ is called the translation dual of O.

accepted.question_text: For a pseudo-oval O(n, n, q) over a field of odd order q, must O always be classical, meaning a classical pseudo-oval in the sense used in the paper?

evidence.quote: 4. Is any O(n, n, q), q odd, always classical?
For n = m such a set O(n, n, q) is called a pseudo-oval or a generalized oval or an [n − 1]-oval of PG(3n − 1, q).

A regular pseudo-oval for which O1 is a conic is called either a pseudo-conic or a classical pseudo-oval, and a regular pseudo-ovoid for which O1 is an elliptic quadric is called a pseudo-quadric or a classical pseudo-ovoid or a classical egg.

accepted.question_text: Let O(n, n, q) = {π_0, …, π_{q^n}} be a pseudo-oval in PG(3n − 1, q). For fixed i, the paper defines an (n − 1)-spread S_i of a skew PG(2n − 1, q) using the tangent space τ_i and the intersections <π_i, π_j> ∩ PG(2n − 1, q). In the even-q case, it also defines an (n − 1)-spread S using the nucleus η and the intersections PG(2n − 1, q) ∩ <η, π_j>. What structural consequences follow when, in the situation described by the source, the spread S, respectively S_i, is regular?

evidence.quote: 5. What can be said if q is even and the (n − 1)-spread S, respectively Si, defined at the beginning of this section, is regular?

Let PG(2n − 1, q) ⊂ PG(3n − 1, q) be skew to πi, i ∈ {0, 1,...,qn}. Further, let τi∩PG(2n−1, q) = ξi,<πi, πj > ∩PG(2n−1, q) = ξj , j = i. Then {ξ0, ξ1,...,ξqn } = Si is an (n − 1)-spread of PG(2n − 1, q). Now let q be even and let η be the nucleus of O(n, n, q). Let PG(2n − 1, q) be skew to η. If ζj = PG(2n − 1, q)∩ < η, πj >, then {ζ0, ζ1,...,ζqn } = S is an (n − 1)-spread of PG(2n − 1, q).

accepted.question_text: Theorem 5.7 states that when q is even, a pseudo-oval O(n, n, q) is classical if and only if it is 2-transitive. Can the same conclusion for odd q be proved without using the classification of finite simple groups?

evidence.quote: 6. Prove, without using the classification of finite simple groups, that Theorem 5.7 also holds for q odd.
Theorem 5.7. The pseudo-oval O(n, n, q), q even, is classical if and only if O(n, n, q) is 2-transitive.

accepted.question_text: For pseudo-ovals O(n, n, q) with q even, Theorem 5.7 assumes 2-transitivity in order to characterize classicality. How far can that hypothesis be weakened—for example, would transitivity alone already force the pseudo-oval to be classical?

evidence.quote: 7. Weaken the hypothesis of Theorem 5.7 for q even (e.g., “what about transitive pseudo-ovals?”).
Theorem 5.7. The pseudo-oval O(n, n, q), q even, is classical if and only if O(n, n, q) is 2-transitive.

accepted.question_text: For the family O(n, m, q) introduced in the paper, where O(n, m, q) is a set of q^m + 1 mutually constrained (n − 1)-dimensional subspaces in PG(2n + m − 1, q), must one always have m ∈ {n, 2n} when q is odd?
accepted.context_brief: Possible parameters for O(n,m,q) in odd characteristic

evidence.quote: 1. Do we have m ∈ {n, 2n} for any O(n, m, q), with q odd?
For n = m such a set O(n, m, q) is called a pseudo-ovoid or a generalized ovoid or an [n − 1]-ovoid or an egg of PG(2n + m − 1, q); a [0]-ovoid of PG(3, q) is just an ovoid of PG(3, q).

accepted.question_text: If O(n, 2n, q) is an egg in even characteristic, is it always regular, in the sense of the paper’s notion of a regular pseudo-ovoid?
accepted.context_brief: Regularity of eggs in even characteristic

evidence.quote: 2. Is any egg O(n, 2n, q), q even, regular?
For n = m such a set O(n, m, q) is called a pseudo-ovoid or a generalized ovoid or an [n − 1]-ovoid or an egg of PG(2n + m − 1, q); a [0]-ovoid of PG(3, q) is just an ovoid of PG(3, q).
Here, we speak of a regular pseudo-oval, respectively a regular pseudo-ovoid.

accepted.question_text: If O(n, 2n, q) is a good egg in even characteristic—meaning there exists an element π such that for every two distinct other elements π′ and π′′, the space <π, π′, π′′> contains exactly q^n + 1 elements of the egg—is the egg necessarily regular?

evidence.quote: 3. Is any good egg O(n, 2n, q), q even, regular?
For n = m such a set O(n, m, q) is called a pseudo-ovoid or a generalized ovoid or an [n − 1]-ovoid or an egg of PG(2n + m − 1, q); a [0]-ovoid of PG(3, q) is just an ovoid of PG(3, q).

An egg O = O(n, 2n, q), respectively a TGQ T(O), is called good at an element π ∈ O if for every two distinct elements π and π′ of O − {π} the (3n − 1)-dimensional space < π, π′, π > contains exactly qn + 1 elements of O; in such a case π is called a good element of O.
Here, we speak of a regular pseudo-oval, respectively a regular pseudo-ovoid.

accepted.question_text: For an egg O(n, 2n, q) in even characteristic, is O always isomorphic to its translation dual O∗(n, 2n, q), where O∗ is the dual egg formed by the tangent spaces of O?

evidence.quote: 4. Is O(n, 2n, q), with q even, always isomorphic to its translation dual O∗(n, 2n, q)?
For n = m such a set O(n, m, q) is called a pseudo-ovoid or a generalized ovoid or an [n − 1]-ovoid or an egg of PG(2n + m − 1, q); a [0]-ovoid of PG(3, q) is just an ovoid of PG(3, q).

The tangent spaces of an egg O(n, m, q), n = m, form an egg O∗(n, m, q) in the dual space of PG(2n+m−1, q). So in addition to T(n, m, q) there arises a TGQ T ∗(n, m, q). The egg O∗(n, m, q) = O∗ will be called the translation dual of O(n, m, q) = O.

accepted.question_text: Given an egg O(n, 2n, q) and its translation dual O∗(n, 2n, q), is it always true that at least one of O or O∗ is good in the sense defined in the paper?
accepted.context_brief: Goodness of an egg or its dual

evidence.quote: 5. Is one of O(n, 2n, q) and O∗(n, 2n, q) always good?

The tangent spaces of an egg O(n, m, q), n = m, form an egg O∗(n, m, q) in the dual space of PG(2n+m−1, q). So in addition to T(n, m, q) there arises a TGQ T ∗(n, m, q). The egg O∗(n, m, q) = O∗ will be called the translation dual of O(n, m, q) = O.

An egg O = O(n, 2n, q), respectively a TGQ T(O), is called good at an element π ∈ O if for every two distinct elements π and π′ of O − {π} the (3n − 1)-dimensional space < π, π′, π > contains exactly qn + 1 elements of O; in such a case π is called a good element of O.

accepted.question_text: For every egg O(n, 2n, q), is there always a pseudo-oval lying on O itself or on its translation dual O∗(n, 2n, q)?
accepted.context_brief: Pseudo-ovals inside an egg or its dual

evidence.quote: 6. Is there always a pseudo-oval on either O(n, 2n, q) or O∗(n, 2n, q)?
For n = m such a set O(n, n, q) is called a pseudo-oval or a generalized oval or an [n − 1]-oval of PG(3n − 1, q).

The tangent spaces of an egg O(n, m, q), n = m, form an egg O∗(n, m, q) in the dual space of PG(2n+m−1, q). So in addition to T(n, m, q) there arises a TGQ T ∗(n, m, q). The egg O∗(n, m, q) = O∗ will be called the translation dual of O(n, m, q) = O.

accepted.question_text: In even characteristic, is every egg O(n, 2n, q) automatically good, in the sense that some element π has the property that every 3n − 1 dimensional space generated by π and two other distinct egg elements contains exactly q^n + 1 egg elements?

evidence.quote: 7. Is O(n, 2n, q), with q even, always good?
For n = m such a set O(n, m, q) is called a pseudo-ovoid or a generalized ovoid or an [n − 1]-ovoid or an egg of PG(2n + m − 1, q); a [0]-ovoid of PG(3, q) is just an ovoid of PG(3, q).

An egg O = O(n, 2n, q), respectively a TGQ T(O), is called good at an element π ∈ O if for every two distinct elements π and π′ of O − {π} the (3n − 1)-dimensional space < π, π′, π > contains exactly qn + 1 elements of O; in such a case π is called a good element of O.

accepted.question_text: Suppose an egg O(n, 2n, q) contains a sub pseudo-conic, where the paper uses “pseudo-conic” for a regular pseudo-oval arising from a conic. Must the egg then be good?

evidence.quote: 8. Is an O(n, 2n, q) with a sub pseudo-conic always good?
A regular pseudo-oval for which O1 is a conic is called either a pseudo-conic or a classical pseudo-oval.

An egg O = O(n, 2n, q), respectively a TGQ T(O), is called good at an element π ∈ O if for every two distinct elements π and π′ of O − {π} the (3n − 1)-dimensional space < π, π′, π > contains exactly qn + 1 elements of O; in such a case π is called a good element of O.

accepted.question_text: Classify the eggs O(n, 2n, q) in even characteristic that contain at least one sub pseudo-oval.
accepted.context_brief: Classification with a sub pseudo-oval present

evidence.quote: 9. Classify the O(n, 2n, q)’s, q even, with at least one sub pseudo-oval.
For n = m such a set O(n, m, q) is called a pseudo-ovoid or a generalized ovoid or an [n − 1]-ovoid or an egg of PG(2n + m − 1, q); a [0]-ovoid of PG(3, q) is just an ovoid of PG(3, q).
For n = m such a set O(n, n, q) is called a pseudo-oval or a generalized oval or an [n − 1]-oval of PG(3n − 1, q).
